Finally, the PseCAST transpososome holocomplex structure highlights a potential allosteric relay mechanism that underlies the target-DNA-dependent catalytic activation of TnsB. In the PEC structure, the β-barrel and C-terminal helical domains of the catalytic TnsB subunits are disordered45. By contrast, both domains are structured in the STC state and interface with the catalytic domain (Fig. 4b) through a network of hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions (Fig. 4f). This is coupled with local structural remodelling of the catalytic domain, resulting in the ordering of an adjacent loop (residues Glu348–Lys369 of TnsB) (Fig. 4g) and an approximately 11-Å concomitant shift of the helix bearing the catalytic Glu340 residue of TnsB (Fig. 4g). The conformational rearrangement marks the transition of the catalytic site from an inactive, post-excision state to an active, strand-transfer configuration that supports Mg2+ coordination and catalytic activity. Consistent with these observations, combined alanine substitutions of Lys567, Gln571 and Asn577 in the C-terminal helical domain of TnsB strongly reduced the transposition activity of PseCAST in E. coli (Fig. 4i). Additional ordering was observed for the N-terminal segment (residues Met1–Pro11) of the TnsA helical domain, which positions the Arg4 residue of TnsA such that it contacts the 5′-terminal phosphate of the cleaved transposon end (Fig. 4c,h), implicating TnsA in TnsB activation. Accordingly, truncation of the TnsA N-terminal segment (ΔMet1–Asn12) resulted in a complete loss of transposition activity (Fig. 4i). Together, the structural observations and their functional validation indicate that the molecular interfaces formed between the C-terminal, β-barrel and catalytic domains of TnsB after binding to the target DNA and TnsC are required to support the integration activity of PseCAST. Both target DNA and TnsC synergistically couple transposase recruitment with domain ordering and catalytic-site remodelling, resulting in the allosteric activation of TnsB for site-specific DNA integration.

Our structural and functional analyses of the PseCAST system comprehensively revealed the molecular mechanism that underlies RNA-guided transposon integration by type I-F CASTs, in which an orchestrated series of interactions and conformational rearrangements couples target recognition with site-specific DNA insertion. Together, these insights support a mechanistic model in which DNA transposition is controlled by a succession of molecular checkpoints (Fig. 5). The formation of the QCascade–TnsC targeting complex requires R-loop completion, enabled by a conformational rearrangement of the Cas8 subunit, including the approximately 90° rotation of the helical bundle domain into a locked conformation. In contrast to the open conformations reported previously for type I-F CAST QCascade complexes9,19,21,37, this locked state positions the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex for binding to TniQ, which facilitates ATP-dependent TnsC assembly on the target DNA by interacting with Cas8 and TniQ. As the locked Cas8 conformation is achieved only with fully matched targets, it acts as a fidelity checkpoint that discriminates against mismatched sites, underpinning the high target specificity of PseCAST. Instead of forming extended filaments as in type V CASTs32,33, PseTnsC assembles into a symmetric heptamer to fully encircle the DNA duplex exiting QCascade. The transposon insertion site is thus defined by the physical footprint and register of the TnsC ring, rather than by TnsB-dependent TnsC depolymerization6,32,33. The initial recruitment of the TnsAB transposase PEC is mediated by the TnsB C-terminal tail hook motifs. As these interactions are dependent on TnsC heptamerization, this step provides another fidelity checkpoint that makes transposition dependent on the correct recognition of the DNA target. Finally, productive target engagement by TnsAB requires conformational ordering of the TnsB β-barrel domain and C-terminal helices, driven by interactions of the TnsB β-barrel domain with the target DNA and the TnsC heptamer. This is coupled with structural remodelling of the TnsB active site into a catalytically competent configuration. Therefore, the TnsC- and target-DNA-dependent catalytic activation of TnsB acts as a final fidelity checkpoint, ensuring that transposon DNA insertion proceeds only once the transposase is correctly anchored to the target DNA. Together, our findings reveal the structural coupling of target DNA engagement and transposase activation, but the precise role of allosteric interactions in the observed conformational rearrangements requires further investigation. We speculate that similar structural coupling is involved in activating TnsAB for transposon excision after interacting with the flanking segments of the donor DNA.

Industry observers note that the Cascade–TniQ complex is guided to the target DNA by base-pairing with its crRNA, leading to the initial formation of a partial R-loop. Coordination of the displaced NTGS by the Cas8 helical bundle is coupled with the transition of the bundle from open to closed, full R-loop formation and the stabilization of the double-stranded PAM-distal target-DNA duplex by the TniQ dimer. TnsC is recruited to the target site, where it assembles into a closed heptameric ring by binding to the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex in the presence of ATP, TniQ and Cas8. At the donor site, excision of the transposon DNA by TnsAB involves the formation of a PEC. The PEC is initially recruited by the TnsC heptamer by interacting with the C-terminal TnsB hooks. Interactions with the target DNA and TnsC result in structural remodelling of the β-barrel and C-terminal helical domains of the interfacing TnsB copies, which is allosterically coupled with a conformational rearrangement of the catalytic domains into an active conformation (the asterisks indicate active TnsB sites). The transposon DNA is integrated by two transesterification reactions catalysed by the active sites of the interfacing TnsBs, covalently linking both transposon 3′ ends to the target DNA with 5-base-pair spacing that results in a target-site duplication (TSD).

Recent findings suggest that directed evolution and structure-guided engineering are powerful complementary strategies for improving CAST activity8,9, recalling previous studies in which structural insights have enabled the rational design of hyperactive variants of the Sleeping Beauty transposase50,51. To provide a structural context for current engineering efforts, we mapped the activity-enhancing substitutions of evoCAST onto the PseCAST holocomplex structure (Extended Data Fig. 9). Two of these, F43S in TnsB and P88T in TnsA, have already been interpreted structurally in the PseTnsAB PEC as potentially facilitating transposon end recognition and stabilizing the cleaved NTGS overhang, respectively. Several of the remaining substitutions in TnsB, which were mostly unresolved in the PEC, can now be interpreted. Y349N, P352T and D396N are found close to the target-DNA substrate, potentially enhancing its binding. Q410K, V526E and Q549R are predominantly surface-facing and thus likely to enhance protein solubility or stability. Q594L, although unresolved in the holocomplex structure, may provide additional hydrophobic interactions to the interface formed between the C-terminal hook and TnsC, which is essential for transposase recruitment. Finally, H464R may promote the interaction between the TnsB β-barrel domain and TnsC through enhanced electrostatic contacts. The substitutions R197I and N314K in TnsC map to the TnsC oligomerization interface and the TnsC–TnsB interface, respectively. Lastly, in addition to the PAM-enhancing mutations N125D and A244N in Cas8, the A410R substitution in the helical bundle likely contacts the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex after R-loop completion (Fig. 5), potentially stabilizing the locked QCascade conformation and promoting TnsC assembly. Together, these insights suggest that evoCAST activity results from the synergistic optimization of DNA binding, intersubunit contacts, folding and solubility. Therefore, future engineering efforts should continue to use both structure-guided and directed-evolution approaches.

In conclusion, the structural findings presented here reveal the molecular mechanisms underpinning RNA-guided transposition by type I CASTs, providing a framework for their further rational engineering for technological applications.

The expression plasmids containing His10–TEV-tagged TniQ and Cas8 (pSL4521), Cas7, Cas6 and the CRISPR array (pSL4522), His6–SUMO–TEV-tagged TnsC (pSL5536) and His6–SUMO–TEV-tagged TnsAB fusion protein (pSL3768) were cloned using standard molecular biology methods including Gibson52 and Golden Gate53 assembly. All plasmids were sequence-verified using whole-plasmid Nanopore sequencing (Genewiz). To clone the expression plasmid containing Cas7, the CRISPR array and Twin-Strep-tagged Cas6 (pMS321), a Twin-Strep-tag54 was added to the C-terminus of cas6 by Gibson assembly: pSL4522 was linearized by PCR using oMS603 and oMS604, and the Twin-Strep-tag was amplified by PCR from a common backbone using the primers oMS605 and oMS606, which contain overhangs compatible with the linearized pSL4522 plasmid. Constructs for expression of His6–MBP-tagged versions of the TnsAB fusion protein and TnsB were generated by PCR amplification of the coding sequence using pSL3768 as template and primer pairs oMS631-632 and oMS634-632, respectively. The PCR products were inserted in the 1C backbone (Addgene; 29654) by ligation-independent cloning55. The His6–MBP-tagged TnsB C-terminal tail (residues 575–613) was prepared by Gibson assembly, using the His6–MBP–TnsB plasmid as a template and the primer pairs oGF181-182 and oGF180-184 to generate the PCR fragments. Plasmids were cloned and propagated in Mach I cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific), purified using the GeneJET plasmid miniprep kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and verified by full-plasmid sequencing or Sanger sequencing (Microsynth). All sequences of primers and parental plasmids used for cloning are provided in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2.

For Cascade–TniQ protein expression, the plasmid pSL4521 encoding His10–TEV–TniQ and Cas8 and the plasmid pMS321 encoding Cas7, Cas6–Twin-Strep and the crRNA were transformed together in 50 μl of E. coli BL21 Rosetta2 (DE3) cells (Novagen), plated on an agar plate and incubated at 37 °C overnight. A single colony was inoculated in 100 ml of Luria broth (LB) to obtain a starter culture. Both the transformation plate and liquid medium were supplemented with 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin, 50 µg ml−1 streptomycin and 33 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol. After overnight growth at 37 °C and 220 rpm, the starter culture was added to eight 750-ml flasks containing antibiotic-supplemented (kanamycin, streptomycin) LB medium to reach a starting optical density at 600 nm (OD600) of 0.05. Cell cultures were grown at 37 °C with shaking at 110 rpm until an OD600 of 0.6 was reached. Protein expression was induced with 0.4 mM isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) for 16 h at 18 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation (4,000g at 4 °C for 30 min) and resuspended in 100 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin and 200 μg ml−1 4-(2-aminoethyl)benzenesulfonyl fluoride (AEBSF). The suspension was lysed using a Maximator cell homogenizer at 1,500 bar and 4 °C. The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000g at 4 °C for 40 min) and applied to three 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in lysis buffer. The columns were washed with 200 ml of HisTrap wash buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole) and eluted with 50 ml of HisTrap elution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 250 mM imidazole). Dithiothreitol (DTT) and ATP were added to the eluted sample to a final concentration of 1 mM each. The sample was added to 7 ml of 50% Strep-Tactin affinity resin suspension (IBA Lifesciences) in HisTrap elution buffer. The mixture was incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 30 min. The protein-bound resin was washed with 70 ml of size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 500 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT) and the sample was eluted with 20 ml of SEC buffer supplemented with 5 mM d-desthiobiotin. Eluted fractions were further purified by SEC using a Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva) column in SEC buffer. Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 10 mg ml−1 using a 30-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use.

According to recent reports, for TnsC expression, the vector pSL5536 encoding His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsC was transformed in 50 μl of E. coli BL21 Star (DE3) cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific), plated on an agar plate supplemented with 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin and incubated at 37 °C overnight. A single colony was inoculated in 100 ml of kanamycin-supplemented LB to obtain a starter culture. After overnight growth at 37 °C and 220 rpm, the starter culture was added to eight 750-ml flasks containing kanamycin-supplemented LB medium to reach a starting OD600 of 0.05. Cell cultures were grown at 37 °C with shaking at 110 rpm until an OD600 of 0.6 was reached. Protein expression was induced with 0.3 mM IPTG for 16 h at 18 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation (4,000g at 4 °C for 30 min). Proteins were purified as described previously for the TnsC of Vibrio cholerae40. A cell pellet (corresponding to four 750-ml liquid cultures) was resuspended in 40 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 5 mM magnesium acetate, 0.2 mM EDTA, 0.1% (v/v) Triton X-100, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin, 200 μg ml−1 AEBSF and 1 μg ml−1 DNase. The suspension was lysed by ultrasonication (Bandelin Sonopuls HD 3200 equipped with a VS 70 T probe, 1 s on–2 s off cycle, at 20% amplitude for 15 min at 4 °C). The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000 g at 4 °C for 45 min) and applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in equilibration buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 10 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT). The columns were washed with 90 ml of equilibration buffer and 50 ml of wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 30 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT), and the proteins were eluted with 10 ml of elution buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 300 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT). Elution fractions were pooled and dialysed overnight against 2 l of dialysis buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 1% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT, 10 mM imidazole) in the presence of 2% (w/w) His6-tagged TEV protease. Any precipitated protein was removed by centrifugation (20,000g at 4 °C for 20 min). The dialysed proteins were applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in equilibration buffer. The columns were washed with 60 ml of equilibration buffer, 90 ml of wash buffer and 50 ml of elution buffer. Flowthrough and initial wash fractions were applied to a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) equilibrated in SEC buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 1% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT). Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 12 mg ml−1 using a 10-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use.

According to recent reports, for the expression of His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsAB (pSL3768), His6–MBP–TEV–TnsAB (pMS329), His6–MBP–TEV–TnsB (pMS331) and His6–MBP–TEV–TnsB(575–613) (pGF189), the procedure described for His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsC was followed, except that 0.4 mM IPTG was used to induce protein expression instead of 0.3 mM. For the purification of untagged TnsAB, TnsB or TnsB(575–613), a cell pellet (corresponding to four 750 ml liquid cultures) was resuspended in 40 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole, 5% glycerol) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin, 200 μg ml−1 AEBSF and 1 μg ml−1 DNase. The suspension was lysed by ultrasonication (Bandelin Sonopuls HD 3200 equipped with a VS 70 T probe, 1 s on–2 s off cycle, at 30% amplitude for 15 min at 4 °C). The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000g at 4 °C for 1 h) and applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in lysis buffer. The columns were washed with 50 ml of lysis buffer, and the proteins were eluted in a stepwise gradient (5%, 20% and 100%) of elution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole, 5% glycerol). Fractions corresponding to the 20% and 100% of elution-buffer concentrations were pooled and dialysed overnight in 2 l of dialysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol, 1 mM DTT) in the presence of 2% (w/w) His6-tagged TEV protease. Dialysed proteins were applied to two 5-ml HiTrap Heparin HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in dialysis buffer, washed with 30 ml of dialysis buffer and eluted in a linear gradient of heparin buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 5% glycerol, 1 mM DTT) over 150 ml (target concentration of heparin buffer: 100%). Peak fractions were pooled and further purified by SEC using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) equilibrated in SEC buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT). Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 15 mg ml−1 using a 50-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use. For the expression and purification of His6–MBP-tagged TnsAB, TnsB and TnsB(575–613), the procedures described for untagged TnsAB, TnsB and TnsB(575–613), respectively, were followed, except that the TEV-cleavage and heparin steps were omitted.

A double-stranded target DNA (dsTarget) was prepared by annealing the synthetic oligonucleotides oMS628 and oMS629 (Supplementary Table 3) in a 1:1 ratio at a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. The pull-down procedure involved mixing the assembly buffer (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 50 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT), 300 pmol of DNA substrate, water and 300 pmol of Cascade–TniQ and incubating this mixture at room temperature for 10 min. Subsequently, ATP or ATPγS (at 1 mM final concentration) was added to the sample, followed by 2,400 pmol of TnsC. The mixture was further incubated at room temperature for 30 min, after which 300 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsB(575–613) or full-length His6–MBP–TnsB was added to the sample to a final volume of 53 μl. After 30 min at room temperature, 147 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP or ATPγS) was added to the sample. Then, 10 μl were withdrawn and mixed with 10 μl of water and 5 μl of SDS dye (225 mM Tris-HCl pH 6.8, 50% (v/v) glycerol, 5% (w/v) SDS, 0.05% (w/v) bromophenol blue, 250 mM DTT) to obtain a 5% input control sample for SDS–PAGE analysis. The sample was mixed with 50 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer and incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1 h. After a short centrifugation (500g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. Subsequently, 25 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose was added to the sample. After centrifugation (14,000g at 4 °C for 2 min), 20 μl of supernatant was mixed with 5 μl of SDS dye to obtain an elution sample for SDS-PAGE analysis. Next, 10 μl of 5% input control and 10 μl of elution sample were loaded on a 10% SDS-PAGE gel (Bio-Rad) for each tested condition. For the control samples Cascade–TniQ–TnsC-minus or MBP–TnsB/AB-minus, the respective SEC buffers were used instead of a protein solution. SDS-PAGE gels were imaged using a ChemiDoc Imaging system (Image Lab Touch software v.4.1, Bio-Rad) and analysed using Image Lab (v.6.1.0, Bio-Rad).

A PseCAST pDonor plasmid was first transformed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells (NEB). Single colonies were inoculated in a liquid culture and the resulting strains were made chemically competent using standard methods. PseCAST pEffector plasmids encoding a crRNA targeting the lacZ locus (crRNA-4) and all CAST subunits were transformed in the resulting strain and plated on double-antibiotic LB agar plates containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin and 100 µg ml−1 spectinomycin. After approximately 20 h of growth, surviving colonies were scraped from the plates, resuspended in fresh LB medium and re-plated on double-antibiotic LB agar plates supplemented with 0.1 mM IPTG to induce PseCAST protein expression. Cells were incubated for an additional 18–20 h, scraped and resuspended in LB medium. Cells were then lysed and integration efficiencies were measured using qPCR as described previously1. Data were plotted and statistical analyses performed in GraphPad Prism (v.11.0.0, GraphPad). Wild-type plasmid sequences, crRNA-4 and oligonucleotides used for qPCR are listed in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2.

Sources indicate that the cryo-EM reconstruction of the QCascade–TnsC targeting complex resulted from an initial attempt to reconstitute the QCascade–TnsC–TnsAB holocomplex. Target- and donor-DNA constructs were prepared by annealing the synthetic oligonucleotides oMS572, oMS573 and oMS576 (target; Supplementary Table 3) and oMS569, oMS570 and oMS571 (donor; Supplementary Table 3) at a 1:1:1 molar ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program involved incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. For the target pot assembly, 10× buffer (200 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1,500 mM KCl, 100 mM MgCl2, 10 mM DTT), water and TniQ–Cascade were gently mixed on ice. The target DNA was added and the sample was incubated at room temperature for 10 min. TnsC and ATP were added to the sample, which was then incubated at room temperature for 15 min. The final target pot volume was 25 μl, containing 4.5 μM of Cascade–TniQ, 4.5 μM of target DNA, 40.5 μM of TnsC, 1 mM ATP, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2 and 1 mM DTT. The donor pot was prepared by mixing 10× buffer, water, ATP, TnsAB and donor DNA to a final volume of 25 μl (containing 18 μM TnsAB, 4.5 μM of donor DNA, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM ATP and 1 mM DTT) and then incubating the mixture at room temperature for 10 min. However, a white insoluble precipitation was observed in the donor pot at this stage and again after mixing with the target pot and incubating at room temperature for 20 min. This was likely due to TnsAB instability under the conditions used. In fact, the donor pot components were not detected in the subsequent cryo-EM analysis. After mixing the target and donor pots, the sample was centrifuged (14,000g at 4 °C for 10 min) and the pellet discarded. Next, 2.5 μl of supernatant was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (30 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 2 s (100% humidity, 4 °C) and plunge-frozen in liquid ethane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI), followed by storage in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on an FEI Titan Krios G3i system (University of Zurich, Switzerland) operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 9,403 movies were acquired at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 47 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 59.672 e− Å−2. EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

In total, 9,403 exposures were imported into cryoSPARC56 live (v.4.3) for real-time processing. After patch-motion and patch-CTF (contrast transfer function) correction, 745,080 particles were identified using blob picker (200–300 Å diameter), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 50 two-dimensional (2D) classes. Next, 416,193 particles were selected and three volumes were generated using ab initio reconstruction. One class yielded a recognizable Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume (108,814 particles) and was used for three-dimensional variability analysis (3DVA; filter resolution: 5 Å; mode: simple); the other two volumes did not contain density for TnsC. Two distinct volumes, resulting from one 3DVA mode, were used as input for heterogeneous refinement to separate the particles of Cascade–TniQ–TnsC from those of Cascade–TniQ only. The two volumes, after a round of non-uniform refinement, were used as inputs for a second heterogeneous refinement, together with one of the volumes from the ab initio multi-class round. This refinement resulted in a volume of Cascade (195,798 particles), Cascade–TniQ (143,494 particles) and Cascade–TniQ–TnsC (76,901 particles). The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume was used for non-uniform refinement after particle re-extraction (76,400 particles), yielding a reconstruction at a resolution of 3.07 Å, as calculated by gold-standard Fourier shell correlation (GSFSC). After particle subtraction, a local refinement of the TnsC heptamer generated a 3.44-Å (GSFSC resolution) map. A composite map was obtained by combining the consensus Cascade–TniQ–TnsC and TnsC-focused volumes using the combine_focused_maps function in Phenix57 (v.2.0-5936). Particles corresponding to Cascade only were used as an input for a 3DVA and heterogeneous refinement as described above. One of the resulting volumes, corresponding to 132,574 particles, yielded a 2.86-Å (GSFSC resolution) Cascade reconstruction after particle re-extraction and non-uniform refinement. The Cascade–TniQ volume was fed twice into a heterogeneous refinement. One of the volumes, corresponding to 50,074 particles, yielded a 3.19 Å (GSFSC resolution) reconstruction after particle re-extraction and non-uniform refinement. All maps and models have been deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) and Protein Data Bank (PDB) (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 1). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 1. Monomeric initial models of Cas6, Cas7, Cas8, TniQ and TnsC were generated using AlphaFold3 (ref. 58). The AlphaFold3 models were docked manually as rigid bodies in the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX59 (v.1.9). The model was real-space refined in Phenix (v.2.0-5936) against the cryo-EM map and then manually in Coot60 (v.0.9.4) using secondary structure, side chain rotamer, Ramachandran and LibG61 nucleic-acid restraints. The nucleic acid model, comprising the crRNA (positions −7 to 52), TGS (positions −60 to 4) and NTGS (positions −4 to 4, 21 to 23 and 34 to 60), was built manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using PDB accession 7U5D (ref. 21) as a starting point. The cryo-EM density was clear enough to distinguish the DNA register. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 1. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1, Adobe). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC complex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1a–f.

The cryo-EM sample of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsB hook recruitment complex was obtained using a pull-down approach. The dsTarget and a double-stranded right-end donor DNA (dsRE) were prepared by annealing synthetic oligonucleotides oMS628-629 and oMS576-630 (Supplementary Table 3), respectively, in a 1:1 ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. The target pot was prepared by adding 1,200 pmol of dsTarget to 100 μl of assembly buffer (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 2 mM DTT), after which KCl solution was added to a final KCl concentration of 230 mM and 1,200 pmol of Cascade–TniQ. The mixture was incubated at room temperature for 10 min, after which ATP and 8,400 pmol of TnsC were added. The sample was then incubated at room temperature for 30 min. The final target pot volume was 200 μl and its buffer composition was 1 mM ATP, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT and 230 mM KCl. A donor pot was prepared by mixing 1,200 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsAB and 1,200 pmol of dsRE substrate. The donor pot was brought to a 20 μl final volume using TnsAB SEC buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 500 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT), mixed with the target pot and incubated at room temperature for 30 min. After adding 30 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP), the sample was mixed with 40 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer and incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1 h. After centrifugation (500 g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. Next, 15 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose was added and the sample was centrifuged (14,000 g at 4 °C for 5 min). The supernatant was isolated by careful pipetting and centrifuged two additional times. A second elution was performed using 20 μl of maltose-supplemented binding buffer, followed by three centrifugation steps as described above. The two eluates were combined into one sample and used to freeze cryo-EM grids. Two and a half microlitres of sample was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (60 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 2.5 s at 100% humidity and 4 °C, plunge-frozen in a cryogenic mixture of liquid ethane and propane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI) and stored in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on a FEI Titan Krios G3i system operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 11,374 movies were acquired at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 37 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 60.947 e− Å−2. EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

Recent findings suggest that in total, 11,374 exposures were imported into cryoSPARC live (v.4.7) for real-time processing. After patch-motion and patch-CTF correction, 329,059 particles were identified using blob picker (200–300-Å diameter), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 50 2D classes. The selected 114,608 particles were used as a training set for Topaz picking (350-Å expected particle diameter, 50 particles per micrograph), yielding 463,242 particles, which were extracted (extraction box size: 500 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 250 pixels) and classified in 150 2D classes. Classes corresponding to 189,451 particles were selected and fed into a two-class ab initio reconstruction, resulting in a junk class and a recognizable Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume (142,343 particles), which was used as input for non-uniform refinement after particle re-extraction. A 2.84-Å (GSFSC resolution) reconstruction was obtained from a final number of 138,834 particles, which was further used for a TnsC-focused local refinement, yielding a 2.96-Å (GSFSC resolution) volume of the heptamer decorated with additional density for each of its seven subunits. A composite map was obtained combining the consensus Cascade–TniQ–TnsC and TnsC-focused volumes using the combine_focused_maps function in Phenix (v.2.0-5936). All maps and models have been deposited in the EMDB and PDB (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 2). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 5. The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC model was rigid-body fitted into the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and adjusted manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using the above-mentioned restraints. The DNA duplex was extended by three nucleotides at the 5′ end of the TGS and by two nucleotides at its 3′ end, with the NTGS extended correspondingly. An initial model of the TnsC heptamer bound to seven TnsB(575–613) copies was generated using AlphaFold3 and docked manually. The model placed the last nine TnsB C-terminal residues at the additional densities of each TnsC subunit. The recognizable density of the bulky TnsB residues Trp605 and Phe612 aided in fitting the TnsB hook in the density. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 2. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsB hook complex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1g–m.

It has been revealed that the cryo-EM sample of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsAB holocomplex was prepared using a pull-down approach. The strand-transfer substrate was prepared by annealing oligos oMS733, oMS734 and oSO146 (Supplementary Table 3) in a 1:1:1 ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM each. The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. Next, 1,000 pmol of substrate, 22.5 μl of assembly buffer A (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 200 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT) and water were mixed with 2,000 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsAB to a final volume of 45 μl, and the sample was kept on ice for 10 min. In the meantime, 35.8 μl (1,000 pmol) of Cascade–TniQ was mixed with 55 μl of assembly buffer B (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 100 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT) and 1.6 μl of water to reduce its KCl concentration to 260 mM. This mixture was added to the initial pot and incubated at room temperature for 10 min. ATP (1 mM final concentration) was added, followed by 7,000 pmol of TnsC, reaching a final volume of 155 μl. The mixture was then incubated at room temperature for 30 min. After the addition of 45 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP), the sample was mixed with 50 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer. The mixture was incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1.5 h, and after centrifugation (500 g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. After adding 25 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose, the sample was centrifuged (14,000 g at 4 °C for 10 min). The supernatant was isolated by careful pipetting and centrifuged two additional times. Next, 2.5 μl of sample was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (60 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 3 s (grid 1) or 2.5 s (grid 2) at 100% humidity and 4 °C, plunge-frozen in a cryogenic mixture of liquid ethane and propane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI) and stored in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on an FEI Titan Krios G3i system operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 43,220 movies were acquired as two separate datasets (dataset 1, 11,964 movies of grid 1; dataset 2, 31,256 movies of grid 2) at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 37 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 60.059 e− Å−2 (dataset 1) or 65.580 e− Å−2 (dataset 2). EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

For both datasets, the exposures were imported to cryoSPARC live (v.4.7) for real-time processing. Datasets 1 and 2 were pre-processed separately. After patch-motion and patch-CTF correction, particles were identified using blob picker (270–290-Å diameter, elliptical blob), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 100 2D classes. Next, 93,462 particles of dataset 1 and 203,735 of dataset 2 were selected for a two-class ab initio reconstruction, which resulted in a Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume and a TnsAB tetramer volume. The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC particles were re-extracted with a bigger box size (extraction box size 1,024 pixels, Fourier-cropped to box size 256 pixels) and used for non-uniform refinement. Using a bigger box revealed additional density at the edge of the particles, corresponding to a flexible TnsAB tetramer next to the TnsC density. This volume was low-pass filtered and used to create masks for particle subtraction. After reducing the box size (extraction box size 700 pixels, Fourier-cropped to box size 350 pixels), the signal for Cascade–TniQ was subtracted from the selected set of particles and the TnsABC moiety was locally refined after aligning the volume to the centre of mass of the TnsABC mask. A 3DVA (filter resolution: 5 Å; mode: simple) yielded one reconstruction with clear density for both TnsC and TnsAB and another with a well-resolved TnsC density but only a weak TnsAB density. The volumes were used as input for two rounds of heterogeneous refinement with the initial set of particles. Next, 49,752 were assigned to the TnsAB-bound TnsC volume, re-extracted (576 pixels) and locally refined, focusing on TnsAB. To adjust the box size for the creation of a composite map, the particles were re-extracted with a larger box-size (700 pixels) and re-aligned to the centre of mass of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC mask, yielding a 49,606-particle set. An ab initio reconstruction, followed by non-uniform refinement, resulted in a Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsAB consensus volume at 3.10 Å GSFSC resolution. Using the consensus map, new masks were generated for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC, TnsC and TnsAB moieties as described above. The masks were used for particle subtraction of the TnsAB signal and local refinement of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC complex. To improve the signal of the TnsB hooks bound to TnsC, a final particle subtraction of the Cascade–TniQ signal was followed by local refinement of TnsC. The TnsAB local refinement was repeated using the final set of 49,606 particles to match the rest of the volumes. This procedure yielded focused cryo-EM maps for the TnsAB tetramer, the hook-bound TnsC heptamer and the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC-hook complex at GSFSC resolutions of 3.36 Å, 3.30 Å and 3.09 Å, respectively. After re-alignment of the TnsAB volume, the global consensus map and the locally refined maps were combined into a composite map using the volume maximum function of ChimeraX (v.1.9). All maps and models have been deposited in the EMDB and PDB (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 3). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 8. The QCascade–TnsC–TnsB hook model was rigid-body fitted in the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and adjusted manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using the above-mentioned restraints. The density corresponding to the tetrameric TnsAB was rigid-body fitted using our previously determined TnsAB PEC structure (PDB 9T7L)45. Missing regions in the protein and nucleic acid chains were built manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) with the aid of an AlphaFold3 model of TnsAB. It was not possible to determine whether the hooks bound to TnsC could be assigned to any of the TnsB copies observed in the structure, as the region between the hook and the last modelled TnsB residue (TnsB(586-604)) is disordered. It should also be noted that the 7:7 TnsC:hook observed stoichiometry probably reflects the excess of bait (His6–MBP–TnsAB) used in pull-down preparations, rather than the physiological interaction ratio, which was observed to be 7:4 in other transpososome structures6,36,41. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 3. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the holocomplex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1n–r.

By Ben Sully | 26 Nov 2026 15:58, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 16:04.

Inter Miami forward Luis Suarez has confirmed he is in talks with the MLS club over a newly introduced contract.

Suarez is in the closing stages of his third full season with Inter Miami after signing on a free transfer at the start of 2024.

The Uruguayan has scored 59 goals in 120 competitive appearances, including 17 strikes in 30 regular-season MLS games this season.

However, as it stands, Suarez is on course to become a free agent when his current deal expires at the end of the calendar year.

In theory, Friday's must-win playoff game against Columbus Crew could be his last, although he has revealed he is in talks over a fresh deal.

"We're already in talks with the club to find the best solution for both sides," Suarez told reporters on Wednesday.

"But honestly, my focus is more on the match against Columbus this Friday than on what will happen in the future.".

Inter Miami are one down in their three-match series against Columbus after falling to a heavy 3-0 defeat at the Nu Stadium on Saturday.

Gonzalo Tapia opened the scoring with a ninth-minute penalty, before Gonzalo Lujan's 36th-minute red card forced Inter Miami to play over 50 minutes with 10 men.

Columbus took full advantage to net two second-half goals to leave Inter Miami requiring a win at the ScottsMiracle-Gro Field to force a deciding game in the first-round tie.

Suarez has made it clear that "the time for excuses is over" as the Herons look to prolong their defence of the MLS Cup.

“It’s clear we are at a club where we have an obligation to win,” Suarez stated.

“If we get eliminated on Friday, it will be a disappointment. We have to be that clear about it.

Recent findings suggest that "The time for excuses is over...it’s time to face reality. If we are eliminated, we will be the first to be self-critical, although we hope that doesn’t happen.

Industry observers note that “I believe the squad are at a point where we understand that it’s time to deliver. This is our final opportunity.

"This format has given us another chance to play this Friday, and it’s the last shot we have to bring the series back home.”.

The visitors experienced disappointment in their last trip to Columbus in September, when they fell to a 2-1 defeat following a stoppage-time winner.

This evening, Ardon Jashari spoke in a press conference ahead of his expected start in AC Milan’s fifth Europa League game.

It has been revealed that tomorrow’s game could be dictated by Jashari, but he’s got big boots to fill. With news of Luka Modric’s injury, the media immediately listed him as the primary candidate to fill the role and Ruben Amorim will oblige by giving him a rare start.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

It has been revealed that it’s as good a chance as any to prove that he is the right man to replace Modric when the veteran eventually leaves San Siro. So, with that date looking very possible to be this summer, this could be the Swissman’s chance to show that he can be the player Milan hoped he’d be when they spent heavily on him in the summer before last.

Speaking alongside Amorim, as MilanNews relays, the Swiss midfielder admitted that he was looking forward to the clash and a chance to prove that he could return to his best.

Are you going back to being the player we saw in Brugge?

“I also like being the kind of player who can help the team with my personality on the pitch.

“If we compare, for example, the competitions now, for us as a team and also for every player like me, it’s key to win matches, and so far we’ve done very well in Serie A. Now we’re starting a different competition; that’s the truth.

“Tomorrow is a great, great opportunity, but also, let’s say, there’s a kind of pressure for all of us. And I think the match against Frosinone is Serie A, it’s a different competition, but still, for all the players, it brought good humour, a good atmosphere, and tomorrow we have to be ready to compete and win the match.”.

Tomorrow you’ll face Freuler, your national teammate….

“I’ll have extra motivation. We talked about this match while we were with the national team. He can’t wait to play against us, and I can’t wait to play against him, too. It’ll be a great match. I can’t wait to meet him and beat him.”.

You lit up on Sunday: what’s your level now? What more can you contribute?

“Good question. I know I can do much better. I think the game against Frosinone was a good one for me, but it’s not the level I want to show. But I’m working every day to be the best version of myself, so the club, the coach, and the fans can see what I’m capable of.”.

What are you working on, and what aspects?

In a recent development, “In the past, where I’ve played, I had a central role in the team, or in the starting eleven. So I always played. I think with Milan I have to learn to be ready even if I don’t always play, and that’s something I haven’t developed in the past.

“I hope that at some point I can be that decisive at Milan too.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that in what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

Recent findings suggest that in what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

Sources indicate that city will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

According to recent reports, in the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

Erling Haaland gets his second of the night, and the game could be back on 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/sFZ0eT2Egz.

It could have been a hat-trick. It could even have been four as Haaland, taking the captain’s armband as Rúben Dias was withdrawn during the interval, clipped the top of the crossbar with a header and then was denied by goalkeeper Matvei Safonov as the striker slid in.

According to recent reports, “Even with 3-0 in the first half, with the amount of chances we created in the second half, we deserved more. Luis [Enrique, PSG’s coach] said at the end of the game that they were quite lucky,” Maresca claimed before being asked whether he would relish facing PSG again, later in this competition. “My feeling is we are there. We are close,” he added.

Sources indicate that did City deserve a draw? No one was predicting that at half-time as they were suffering as comprehensive a defeat as was inflicted by the commission. Accused of “sham” contracts to inflate income, this was a sham of a performance, made all the more emphatic because of how brilliant PSG, and their exceptional 21-year-old winger Désiré Doué, were.

Désiré Doué with a brilliant finish from range to give PSG an early lead in Manchester 😮‍💨 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/Uwilx7I37H.

There is a certain irony that it was PSG who inflicted this defeat, ending City’s run of eight wins from eight in all competitions under Maresca.

It was a meeting of two clubs empowered more than any other by the riches of Gulf states: Abu Dhabi versus Qatar. Both have also had their run-ins over money. Both were sanctioned, but escaped full bans by Uefa for breaching financial fair play rules.

The question, also, was: would the eighth meeting of these clubs in the Champions League in the last 11 seasons be the last for some time?

Sources indicate that so we should savour it and we did. That included Pep Guardiola on his first return to the Etihad – in a sign of solidarity – after quitting at the end of last season. Not that he savoured much of what he saw as PSG dominated City to such an extent that their fans adopted the “Poznan” celebration and the home supporters were silenced.

City could have gone in front before they conceded with the erratic Safonov – who was Gianluigi Donnarumma’s understudy and has become his unlikely replacement – punching a corner against his own crossbar before Antoine Semenyo shot the rebound over.

Then PSG ran all over City. They broke far too easily and scored far too easily. Not once, but twice, to go 2-0 up.

For the first, PSG countered, with City struggling to cover, and Doué caught out Donnarumma with a low shot inside his right-hand post from 22 yards.

It has been revealed that then PSG sliced through City’s defence with Ousmane Dembélé scooping the ball across the area to Doué who returned it back. Dembélé stooped to head home.

Ousmane Dembélé doubles PSG's lead just 2 minutes after they scored the first 🤯 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/MxhJ3oCWpC.

After Achraf Hakimi headed against the inside of a post and City could not clear, the ball came back with Warren Zaïre-Emery flicking on Maghnes Akliouche’s cut-back. It ran to Vitinha who slammed in a first-time shot. It was the first time City had ever conceded three goals at home in the first half of this competition.

Vitinha with a BEAUTY to put PSG three up after just 30 minutes 🥵 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/vgqkI6kI3h.

Maybe it was too easy. Maybe City could not continue to be so dominated but it was as if a switch was flicked when the teams returned. The chances came for City. Enzo Fernández should have scored from a close-range header and Haaland did, glancing in an inswinging Ndiaye cross.

Finally the City fans found their voices but then they were silenced. What a calamity for Donnarumma as he got a hand to Akliouche’s shot on the turn, but only palmed the ball up in the air before it bounced into the net.

Recent findings suggest that but City did not stop. Nuno Mendes headed Josko Gvardiol’s flick off the line, Fernández hit a post before Bouaddi set up Haaland and he swept the ball past Safonov.

Erling Haaland gets his second of the night, and the game could be back on 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/sFZ0eT2Egz.

In a recent development, there was time for PSG to miss a penalty, with Donnarumma comfortably saving Ferran Torres’s weak effort as City bravely continued to push. They lost, but it did not quite feel like that.

Recent findings suggest that I think our start was quite good until the first goal. Then we conceded the second after one [more] minute and that created bad feelings so we struggled.

Second half we were much, much, much better and we probably deserved even something more.

It was strange to be honest because until the first goal we were in the game. We created things, didn’t concede and then the first goal led to the second one. When you concede two goals in two minutes it could [get] even worse.

At half-time we adjust something, didn’t lose our balance and in the second half we created enough to deserve something more. We adjusted the way we were pressing, something on the ball [too].

We lost the balance [by conceding the second goal]. Even at zero-three we created enough in the second half and Luis stated afterwards that they had been quite lucky.

[A message for the fans?] We feel sorry for the first half but I think we’re quite happy now. Significant game on Saturday [Ipswich at home at 3pm].

Both Arsenal and Barcelona had shorter prices than PSG to win the Champions League. Now it’s only Barcelona but I would say even they are not as good as PSG.

I doubt Guardiola will speak publicly but let’s wait and see.

After a PSG performance in the first half that was as good as any I’ve seen in the past 10 years, Manchester City stiffened midfield in the second and went toe-to-toe to play their part in a basketball game with crosses and shots raining down on the PSG goal.

PSG have managed this last few minutes well, making key tackles and interceptions.

Pacho cuts out a pass to stop Semenyo pouncing.

PSG have dropped back in numbers and City are probing away.

Anderson, looking for Haaland from the left with a right-foot inswinger, overcooks it and Safonov comes off his line to catch.

Haaland meets Nunes daisycutter of a cross having been sent to the byline with his outstretched left leg as he slides in at the back post and Safonov sprawls to save on the goalline again. Should have scored but then again he was right at the extent of his reach when he made the connection.

Attempts on goal now number 36 after Kvaratskhelia’s tepid effort is saved by Donnarumma then Khusanov makes a last gasp tackle to stop Ferran Torres converting Joao Neves’s sensational pass.

Good evening, and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Manchester City and Paris St-Germain, champions in 2025 and 2026 and favourites to become only the fourth club, after Real Madrid (who have done it twice), Ajax and Bayern Munich to win a hat-trick of European Cups.

After Manchester City’s conviction by an independent commission on 114 charges of financial malpractice in contravention of Premier League rules, finding the right tone to use to cover their matches during their appeal is difficult. While they are in limbo, the rest of English football is in purgatory and although Gary Neville, the Pope of Pilsworth, in unsurprisingly hyperbolic fashion has stated he would prefer not to cover City’s games in future, that is not an indulgence a serious news organisation would countenance. They have to be covered and the challenges addressed.

Having noted that, in this format of a rolling report on the old minute-by-minute template, I think we have to cover the controversy and its implications in the whole during the build-up and keep an eye on reaction and references to it during the run of play. But I don’t think it would serve anyone to take the stance during the live coverage that anything that is happening on the field is unimportant, redundant and ultimately void because of the guilty verdicts, and hence adopt a flippant tone. I propose once the match starts to treat it as a match while not ignoring the context.

The Walcott has urged Arsenal star Noni Madueke to ‘substantial himself up more’ after Mikel Arteta revealed last night’s man of the match was frustrated in the wake of a 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund.

For the second match in succession, the Premier League champions threw away a lead and squandered numerous chances to record a convincing win.

Viktor Gyokeres opened the scoring with a blistering strike in the 10th minute, but the Sweden international, like many of his teammates, was profligate thereafter.

Ultimately, the Gunners were forced to settle for a point following Maximilian Beier’s second half equaliser and Mikel Arteta’s side are now likely to require two wins from their remaining three group stage games to secure a top eight finish and avoid a two-legged play-off in the Fresh Year.

Sources indicate that madueke, meanwhile, walked away with the man of the match accolade after another lively display. The England international has been to the fore in recent weeks and, in the absence of Bukayo Saka, appears to have won the faith of the manager who raised eyebrows with his decision to sanctionthe decision to sign him from Chelsea in a £52million deal 18 months ago.

The 24-year-old was, however, far from pleased with a display that failed to help yield a win that Arsenal’s dominance deserved, according to Arteta.

‘Again he was really good, but if you were in the dressing room (you would see) he is not satisfied because he knows he had so many situations again that we can put the ball in the net or finish the action much better,’ said the Arsenal boss.

‘But again he was a real threat, he was super connected to the game with and without the ball. He was a real threat.’.

Walcott, meanwhile, agreed with his former Arsenal teammate and believes Madueke is showing signs that he is capable of maintaining a regular starting spot.

Rodman was set to take part in the 2026 CONCACAF W Championship window in Texas, but has now pulled out due to what US Soccer called 'a minor shoulder injury' in a statement announcing the roster move.

It has been revealed that the statement says the injury occurred during the 2026 NWSL Championship Game last Saturday, where Rodman and the Washington Spirit fell 2-1 to the Kansas City Current. US Soccer has replaced Rodman with Gotham FC winger Jaedyn Shaw.

Rodman's removal comes hours after the Daily Mail was first to report on her split from the American tennis star.

The American sporting couple began dating around March 2025, frequently supporting one another at their various events, but have recently decided to call time on their relationship.

Industry observers note that their conflicting work schedules and constant travel made it too challenging for the couple to continue maintaining their relationship, the Daily Mail understands. However, the pair are believed to remain close, despite their split.

How England could line up without Harry Kane as Thomas Tuchel given unusual solution (exclusive)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Knapton | 26 Nov 2026 16:00, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 16:00.
  • England manager Thomas Tuchel has been told to consider an unusual solution to Harry Kane's injury absence if the Three Lions captain misses March's Nations League quarter-final with Norway.
  • Tuchel and co are sweating over the fitness of the Ballon d'Or winner after he was ruled out for a 'few months' with a serious ankle injury, sustained in Bayern Munich's 1-1 Bundesliga draw with FC Koln earlier this month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 26 Nov 2026 16:00, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 16:00.

England manager Thomas Tuchel has been told to consider an unusual solution to Harry Kane's injury absence if the Three Lions captain misses March's Nations League quarter-final with Norway.

Tuchel and co are sweating over the fitness of the Ballon d'Or winner after he was ruled out for a 'few months' with a serious ankle injury, sustained in Bayern Munich's 1-1 Bundesliga draw with FC Koln earlier this month.

Kane had to undergo surgery to correct the torn ligament, and there is a chance that he could now sit out the reunion with World Cup quarter-final foes Norway, whom the Three Lions face at the end of March 2027.

Tuchel has a plethora of alternative centre-forward options at his disposal, including Dominic Calvert-Lewin, Dominic Solanke, Ivan Toney, Ollie Watkins and Championship star Will Lankshear.

However, ex-England forward Brian Deane has exclusively told Sports Mole that Tuchel could instead consider using either Jude Bellingham or Morgan Rogers as a false nine rather than deploying a pure centre-forward.

“It is difficult because I do not think England have another centre-forward who can do exactly what Harry Kane does," Deane said. "He is not the quickest, but he is intelligent, drops into pockets and allows the team to rotate around him. He has earned the right for the manager to build that structure.

“Dominic Calvert-Lewin is very good at holding the ball up, bringing others into play and competing in the air. Whether he would score the same types of goals as Kane is another question.

In a recent development, “Solanke has the ability, but I am not convinced about his confidence at the moment. The England shirt can weigh heavily.

“Ivan Toney has a strong all-round game, is excellent in the box and is one of the best penalty-takers around. The question would be how he adjusts to the tempo of international football from the league he is playing in.

“Will Lankshear is perhaps a little inexperienced. Bringing him into the squad is one thing; asking him to lead the line ahead of those other players is another.

“Tuchel might decide not to use a conventional centre-forward. He could put Jude Bellingham or Morgan Rogers further forward and approach it differently. It is very difficult to replicate Kane. He has done amazingly well and is almost irreplaceable.”.

According to data from Transfermarkt, Bellingham has only made one club appearance as an out-and-out centre-forward, compared to 23 for Rogers during his career.

If Deane's prediction comes true and Tuchel does opt for a false-nine approach, the Chelsea man should therefore be at the head of the queue for striking duties, especially having also featured in that role for the Blues already this season against Tottenham Hotspur.

Bellingham has licence to continue in the number 10 role as a result, and Rogers being moved centrally opens the door for a fit-again Bukayo Saka to reclaim his place on the right flank.

However, there is every chance that Kane will recover in time to face Norway, aiming to build on an unparalleled record of 93 goals in 127 matches for his country.

Brian Deane was speaking to Sports Mole on behalf of BetWright.

Jobe Bellingham revealed one of Borussia Dortmund’s coaches was responsible for identifying a ‘mismatch’ that helped his side earn a valuable Champions League point against Arsenal.

The Gunners could’ve been out of sight at half-time but had only Viktor Gyokeres’ spectacular early goal to show for their superiority.

Bundesliga table toppers Dortmund, were a different side immediately after the break and claimed a deserved equaliser through Maximilian Beier.

Dortmund’s physical approach and man-to-man system gradually saw them take control and they were millimeters from taking the lead when Bellingham was ruled offside and saw his close-range effort disallowed.

The 21-year-old was substituted shortly afterwards as was the Arsenal star he had be targeting having been instructed to make the most of a physical mismatch.

‘One of the coaches pointed out to me that I was against Myles [Lewis-Skelly],’ he explained on Amazon Prime Video.

‘For the long ball – I don’t want to say a mismatch – but I’m obviously bigger.

Tickets for the Lions' second-round game at home to Notts County went on sale on Thursday, with queues stretching into the car park.

The game is the final match of second-round weekend, and takes place after the draw, meaning both sides could go into it knowing they will have a tie against Premier League opposition if they win.

Industry observers note that "Do you remember when England got to the World Cup semi-finals?" mentioned Guiseley director Peter Gable. "The next day, the mood of the nation was lifted.

"After the Sutton game (when the Northern Premier League side knocked out Conference opposition in round one), I'd like to think that everyone woke up on a Monday morning thinking, 'Guiseley did it and we're in the next round.'.

"We've got a tough match against Notts County, but they won't be relishing coming here.

"There's a banana skin in every round and we'd like to think we might be that banana skin.

"The third-round draw is done before the match so Guiseley or Notts County will play and it could be anyone – Liverpool, Arsenal, Tottenham, even some of the Championship teams,.

"Just to be in the third round draw means a lot to the club, the staff, the management, the volunteers, and of course, the supporters.”.

The Sutton game was played on an afternoon Leeds, Bradford and Huddersfield Town were at home, but TNT Sports have ensured this one stands alone – helpful for those with split loyalties like Leeds season-ticket holder Gable and those in the queue wearing Bradford or Leeds shirts.

It has been revealed that "We're fairly confident of selling out," he said. "Tickets will be on sale again at the Whitby match (on Saturday). But it's lovely to see a big queue, a lot of excited faces.

"Now Leeds are back in the Premier League and they're not playing every Saturday we have noticed our attendances are slowly rising.

Industry observers note that "We've got a great team at the minute, they don't know when to give in. We've got a great manager in Ian (Richards) and things are really looking rosy.

In a recent development, "The main target this season, of course, is promotion but a cup run? Can't beat it.

"We've got prepares for a newly introduced stand at the cricket club end. There's loads of infrastructure that we need to do and we've got some nice plans, so the money from this cup run will be a big help.".

Shaun Wright-Phillips: Chelsea star must make himself ‘hard to ignore’ for Xabi Alonso

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Estevao burst onto the scene across an eye-catching opening campaign with Chelsea having joined the club from Palmeiras in the summer of 2025, racking up eight goals and four assists for the Blues.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Chelsea and England star Shaun Wright-Phillips has urged Estevao to fight tooth and nail for a starting spot at Stamford Bridge and make himself ‘hard to ignore’ under Xabi Alonso.

Estevao burst onto the scene across an eye-catching opening campaign with Chelsea having joined the club from Palmeiras in the summer of 2025, racking up eight goals and four assists for the Blues.

A serious hamstring tear brought Estevao’s debut season to a premature end, though, a devastating blow that saw him miss out on a place in Brazil’s squad at this year’s World Cup.

Just days after Estevao sustained his injury, Chelsea decided to call time on Liam Rosenior’s turbulent managerial spell – and it has proven difficult for the 19-year-old to work himself back into the side since Alonso took charge.

The teenager had been limited to only two starts in the Carabao Cup approaching late October and rumours were beginning to circulate that he had grown frustrated with his peripheral role, with Barcelona reportedly keeping tabs on the situation.

However, Joao Pedro’s absence over the last month-and-a-half has created an opportunity for Estevao in Alonso’s attack and the youngster has started two of Chelsea’s last three games.

A humbling 4-1 defeat at the hands of Leeds may not have been what Estevao had in mind for his return, though, following a substitute appearance at Sunderland, and he will no doubt be desperate to banish those memories with a strong performance versus Nottingham Forest on Friday night.

Asked if he felt that Estevao still had a major future at Chelsea under Alonso, Wright-Phillips told Metro, courtesy of kwiff: ‘It’s a hard one, because it seems like players at Chelsea outlive the managers, which is sad to say.

‘That’s where modern football is going at the minute. It seems like players are outlasting coaches.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

‘But in general, that’s more of a tactical thing, in that Xabi plays more with wing-backs.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, ‘If you play Estevao, you want him in the front three. Chances come in random ways, so he will get his chance again, and he has to do what he did the other day.

‘When he came on, I thought he was flying: not the weekend just gone, the weekend before that [against Sunderland. He came on and played really, really well.

‘So that’s him saying, “Look, I’m good enough to stay in your squad.” If he continuously does that, it becomes hard to ignore.’.

Another player whose development has hit something of a stumbling block in recent months is Malo Gusto, who, like Estevao, has found regular game-time hard to come by this season.

Reports just last week indicated Gusto could be open to the prospect of leaving Chelsea, with Manchester United understood to be among the right-back’s admirers.

Sources indicate that but when asked if it could be time to move Gusto on should a suitable offer come in for the Frenchman, Wright-Phillips replied: ‘Who do you replace him with? I think Gusto is a really fantastic player.

‘He might not be happy, which is understandable, because before Xabi came, when the other managers were there, his playing time was a lot greater, because it was either him or Reece James.

In a recent development, ‘Reece James has had bad luck, he’s injured quite a lot, so Gusto got to play a lot. Whereas now, I think he’s better than a bit-part player, to be honest.

‘I haven’t watched him enough this season to turn around and say he should definitely be starting, but from what I saw of him last year and the type of player he is, I’d have him in my team at the drop of a hat, because I don’t think there are many right-backs out there that are gettable of that standard.’.

Chelsea splashed out in the region of £350million on fresh signings in the summer transfer window, including Morgan Rogers, who commanded a club-record fee of £117m when he joined from Aston Villa.

There were signs that the Blues were reaping the rewards of their significant spending in a promising start to the 2026/27 campaign, with Alonso’s all-star front three firing on all cylinders.

An injury to Joao Pedro has coincided with a concerning dip in results, though, and Alonso’s men were targeted with a chorus of boos as they exited the pitch following their latest setback on Saturday.

‘I think at the very beginning he indicated why he’s there, and at the minute it seems to have plateaued a bit. I don’t know what that’s from,’ Wright-Phillips remarked when asked what he had made of Alonso’s start to managerial life in the Premier League, with Chelsea languishing down in eighth.

‘Playing as many games as they have, with the internationals that have come in the way they’ve come in, it feels like the Champions League is every week; it feels like it’s the Carabao Cup or something every week at the minute.

‘It’s going to take a bit of time for the players to get used to that change, where every game is a substantial game now for everybody; literally every game comes around very quick.

‘I think those clubs will settle down and get it together because they’re lucky to have the players within that squad to do that.’.

Pressed on whether there were any areas of the squad in need of strengthening in January, Wright-Phillips responded: ‘I’m not sure they need midfielders. I would say if they had two, or even one, solid defenders who can teach the other young ones there, that would be more than enough.

Sources indicate that ‘Chelsea have got an amazing squad. They’re missing that rock at the back; who will fight and die for everybody, because that rubs off on the team.

‘You might not like him, but that attitude and mentality will naturally rub off on you. Someone in the Thiago Silva mould.

Sources indicate that ‘They need to learn; they’re learning from each other. They’re good players, but to get to the top, most younger players and defenders learn off somebody with a lot more experience.’.

Switching his focus to the title race, Wright-Phillips, who represented Manchester City, Chelsea and QPR during his playing days, picked out Brighton as this year’s surprise package.

And while they were beaten in stoppage time by Hull City at the weekend, the ex-England winger is confident the Seagulls remain one of Arsenal’s ‘main challengers’.

‘No disrespect to Arsenal, but the best club for me in the Premier League this season, to watch and for output, is Brighton,’ Wright-Phillips – a Premier League winner with Chelsea in 2006 – explained.

‘Brighton are probably playing the best, but they’re not at the top of the league.

‘It can change and go a different way. I don’t think Arsenal are playing that well, and I don’t think City have played that well, but they’re the two teams that know how to get results when they aren’t playing to the level they know their maximum is.

‘Unfortunately for City, that hasn’t happened in the last four games, which is something they have to deal with and turn around.

‘The Christmas period is the right time to possibly do it, because all the games come quick and fast and the league table can change a dozen times in that time.

Sources indicate that ‘The main challengers to Arsenal would be Brighton and Manchester City as it stands. They’re the ones with the points on the board.

‘Until people start putting the points on the board, which is turning around, you’re seeing Liverpool sneak back up the table.

‘There will be other challenges as well, but leading into this Christmas period, I would say Arsenal’s challenger right now is Brighton and Manchester City.

‘Brighton, I think, are the only team to beat both of those two teams and do it nicely as well. It wasn’t a smash and grab.’.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Both are in their second spells at the club and the former had his best year at Oakwell during the German's memorable first season as head coach in 2018-19.

Given what the Reds are currently experiencing, that magnificent promotion campaign must seem like a world away.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The pair are now fighting fires at the wrong end of League One; beleaguered Barnsley currently prop up the table following a wretched 11-match winless streak.

In his second coming at Oakwell, Stendel named McGeehan, a player he rates and trusts, as his on-pitch leader in the summer.

So far this term, the Reds chief has largely been spared the ire of increasingly agitated followers; most have elected to vent their frustration toward the Oakwell hierarchy instead.

But given Barnsley's atrocious autumnal numbers - two points taken from the last available 33 - chatter is also starting to centre on the German's position.

For McGeehan, the club's top-scorer with nine goals, it provides a personal element in his quest to help the stricken Reds change the narrative of a hard season.

He also shares sympathy with Stendel, given Barnsley's tendencies to continually shoot themselves in the foot - which he feels has nothing to do with the head coach.

A case in point was at Bradford City on Tuesday, when all three of the visitors' concessions were self-inflicted.

Speaking ahead of the crunch trip to fellow strugglers AFC Wimbledon, McGeehan said: "I think coming in after the game, a lot of the boys were saying: 'the gaffer's going to be pulling his hair out' because that was just down to the players' mistakes.

"And it's happened too many times this season, we've made poor individual errors that have led to goals and caused us to lose games we probably shouldn't have.

"We want to get a positive result for everyone at the club.

In a recent development, "But obviously the gaffer's someone I've worked with before and you can see it completely consumes him. He wants the very best and he's passionate to get Barnsley into a good place, as we all are. We're all fighting together.

Industry observers note that "It can all change very rapidly. But it starts with us on the pitch getting a positive result. This poor run's lasted way too long and we've got to draw a line in the sand.

"Obviously, there's a lot of positive things that we've done in games and it's just trying to get that game where it clicks and then you go from there.".

The busy run to the turn of the year looks critical for Barnsley, currently four points adrift of safety, with several fixtures coming up against sides around them.

Should the Reds manage to chip away with some much-needed wins, January will come into sharp focus.

Recruiting a defensive lieutenant and an experienced leader of the line are surely two huge priorities for a side that is right now dangerously weak in both boxes, where games are decided, despite getting other things right elsewhere.

According to recent reports, on the importance of bringing in some seniority in the new year at the sharp ends of the pitch, McGeehan observed: "Potentially. You can look at that obviously when you're not doing well, you sort of start to pick apart different things.

"At the start of the season, when we started quite well, you sort of think: 'oh, we've got a youthful, energetic side'.

Recent findings suggest that "There's always two ways you can spin it. I've seen experienced players make mistakes for goals and be short of confidence as well. January will come and teams always make signings but all we are concentrating on is now and do what we can with what we've got.

"We've got some really good players here and hopefully we can turn the corner. It's everyone sticking together and trying to fight. It's the only way out of this.".

McGeehan admits that listening to opposing managers and pundits continuing to label Barnsley as a good footballing side is becoming 'boring'.

Recent findings suggest that for his part, Stendel concurs, adding: "This is easy to say when you win the game and keep the points. I don't like it.".

The Reds boss also has no truck with the disquiet of supporters either.

It spilled over at the final whistle at Valley Parade on Tuesday with chants of 'You're not fit to wear the shirt' aimed at players.

The Oakwell boss, who confirmed that Reyes Cleary is not yet back in training, with Cieran Slicker and Makenzie Kirk having issues ahead of the weekend, added: "When you are upset, you say things like that. This is not different at Barnsley to other clubs in the world.

In a recent development, "I also have to support and protect my team. They are trying to do their best. It is not enough at the moment for the expectation of what we have as a club and also not for the supporters.".
